title: Interzone and the Word Lines: the Exterminator, the Cut-Up, and the Virus Called Language
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: St. Louis, birth on Pershing Avenue
stops.date_confidence: attested. The address 4664 Pershing Avenue is Burroughs's own in 'St. Louis Return' (1965); the street was Berlin Avenue until the First World War. The pool's chronology lens carried a latitude some 400 metres too far south; the 4600 block at this longitude sits at 38.6466 per OpenStreetMap, and that is used here.
stops.campa: William Seward Burroughs II is born in a three-story brick house in the Central West End, second son of Mortimer Burroughs and grandson of the man whose adding machine taught American offices to count without thinking. The family has money but not the fortune the name implies; the patent went out of the family before the boy arrived. He grows up with a nurse, a maid, and a gardener, in a house he will describe in his first novel as a solid, three-story, brick house in a large Midwest city. The street outside is called Berlin Avenue until the war renames it.
suggested_refs: 4664 Pershing Avenue, St. Louis, described by Burroughs in 'St. Louis Return' (1965)

stops.name: Los Alamos Ranch School, the boy sent west
stops.date_confidence: attendance 1929-1931 attested (Morgan, Literary Outlaw; Miles, Call Me Burroughs); month and day default to 01 for the start of the school year. The pin is Fuller Lodge, the school's surviving building. The pool's geography lens placed a pet ferret here; the ferret belongs to his Harvard rooms in the early 1930s and has been moved there.
stops.campa: Sent west at fifteen for his sinuses and his temperament, the boy boards at a ranch school in the Jemez foothills where the students sleep on unheated porches, ride horses, and wear shorts through the New Mexico winter. He reads Wilde and De Quincey, keeps a diary about another boy, and writes home begging to be taken out. In his second year they take him out. Sixteen years later the government buys the mesa, the lodge, and the horse pastures, and builds the atomic bomb on the ground where he learned to ride.
suggested_refs: Fuller Lodge, Los Alamos, the Ranch School building requisitioned for the Manhattan Project in 1943

stops.name: Harvard, the degree and the revolver
stops.date_confidence: matriculation 1932 and the A.B. in English literature in 1936 are attested (Harvard College records; Britannica). Month and day default to 01. The live ferret and the pistol kept in his rooms are reported by Morgan and Miles rather than by any institutional record.
stops.campa: He takes rooms at Harvard and a degree in English literature. The final clubs do not want him and he despises them back. He keeps a revolver and a live ferret in his rooms, and reads anthropology on his own account, outside the syllabus. What four years inside the institution teach him is how it decides who is licensed to speak and whom the rules are for. He graduates in 1936. His parents settle two hundred dollars a month on him, and go on paying it, in one form or another, for the next twenty-five years.
suggested_refs: Harvard College class records for the A.B. of 1936

stops.name: Vienna, medicine at the old Allgemeines Krankenhaus
stops.date_confidence: autumn 1936 to 1937, documented as the period 'Vienna 1936/37' (Thomas Antonic, 'Amongst Nazis: William S. Burroughs in Vienna 1936/37', European Beat Studies Network). The pool's chronology lens dated the enrolment to 1937, a year late; the geography lens has 1936-1937 and is followed. The pin is the old medical faculty in Alsergrund, not the modern Medical University campus opened in 1994.
stops.campa: He enrols in medicine at Vienna, in the old hospital complex in Alsergrund, drawn by a long fascination with disease and with the body understood as a machine that fails. What he finds on that campus in the autumn of 1936 is Nazi students beating Jewish ones in the corridors and a faculty that looks away. He lasts a matter of months. In the refugee circles of the city he meets Ilse Herzfeld Klapper, a German Jewish woman out of Berlin who cannot leave Europe on her own passport and has nothing to trade for one.
suggested_refs: Thomas Antonic, 'Amongst Nazis: William S. Burroughs in Vienna 1936/37'
sources: Thomas Antonic, European Beat Studies Network

stops.name: Dubrovnik, the refugee circle in the walled port
stops.date_confidence: Dubrovnik is where Burroughs and Klapper met and where she later sailed from; month and day are an ordering device only. The pool's chronology lens placed the marriage here; RealityStudio, 'The White Russian Countess: On Ilse Herzfeld Klapper and Her Marriage to William Burroughs', places the wedding in Athens, and this file follows it.
stops.campa: The circle he has been moving in scatters south to the Dalmatian coast, where Klapper is living among other refugees inside the walls. They are friends and nothing else; she is thirteen years older and interested in neither romance nor rescue on those terms. What she needs is an American husband and the non-quota visa that comes with him. Burroughs is twenty-three, with a Harvard degree, an allowance, and no plans. He agrees. On the fifth of January 1939 she sails from this harbour on the MS Vulcania and lands in New York on the nineteenth.
suggested_refs: RealityStudio, 'The White Russian Countess: On Ilse Herzfeld Klapper and Her Marriage to William Burroughs'

stops.name: Athens, the marriage that is a document
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by RealityStudio, 'The White Russian Countess', which corrects the widely repeated claim that the wedding took place in Dubrovnik.
stops.campa: On the second of August they are married in Athens: a clerk, a form, two signatures, and no ceremony either of them afterwards describes as one. It is the first piece of state machinery Burroughs operates deliberately, and it does exactly what he intends. The marriage produces a visa and produces nothing else. They divorce after the war and remain friends for the rest of her life. He is nowhere on record calling it a good deed. In later interviews he treats it as a technical matter.
suggested_refs: The 1939 non-quota immigrant visa issued to Ilse Herzfeld Klapper Burroughs

segments.name: Exterminator: Chicago, Columbia, and the Valley

stops.name: Buena Park, Chicago: the exterminator's route
stops.date_confidence: the 1942 exterminator job and the psychiatric discharge from the Army are attested (RealityStudio, 'The Exterminator, They Called Him'; Chicago Reader). Month and day default to 01. The pool's geography lens gave a coordinate some 1.5 km northwest of Buena Park; the neighbourhood pin from OpenStreetMap is used instead.
stops.campa: Discharged from the Army on psychiatric grounds after his mother's intervention, he takes a room in Buena Park and work as an insect exterminator, going through North Side kitchens with a hand duster of yellow pyrethrum powder. He learns the tenement economy from underneath: which landlords pay, which roaches survive which poison, what a building smells like when nobody is watching it. The job lasts less than a year. Thirty years later he is still introducing himself to interviewers as an exterminator, and in 1973 he puts the word on the cover of a book.
suggested_refs: Exterminator! (1973), the story collection drawn from the Chicago year

stops.name: Columbia and the West End Bar, the circle forms
stops.date_confidence: 1943 attested for the meeting with Ginsberg and Kerouac through Lucien Carr (Wikipedia; Untapped New York; Columbia Magazine, 'The Last Beat'). Month and day default to 01; the meeting was a process rather than a dated event.
stops.campa: In New York he falls in with the circle around Lucien Carr at Columbia: Allen Ginsberg at nineteen, Jack Kerouac at twenty-one, and Joan Vollmer, a journalism student with a Benzedrine habit and the fastest talk in the room. Burroughs is approaching thirty, older than any of them, and arrives with a Harvard degree, a monthly allowance, a working knowledge of Spengler and Korzybski, and a suit. They treat him as a teacher and he behaves like one, handing Ginsberg reading lists. The bar is the West End, on Broadway at 114th Street.
suggested_refs: The West End Bar, 2911 Broadway, meeting place of the Columbia circle

stops.name: West 115th Street, the shared apartment
stops.date_confidence: 1945 attested for the shared apartment with Kerouac, Edie Parker and Joan Vollmer (Wikipedia, 'William S. Burroughs'); month and day default to 01. The pin is the 400 block of West 115th Street and is approximate to the street rather than the door.
stops.campa: He moves into a shared apartment on West 115th Street with Kerouac, Edie Parker, and Joan Vollmer, and by degrees into Vollmer's bed and her habits. She is on Benzedrine inhalers cracked open and soaked in coffee; he is beginning on morphine. They talk all night and each claims to know what the other is thinking. Neither of them is the person the other set out to find. The household runs on amphetamine and secondhand books, and the rent comes from their families.
suggested_refs: The 419 West 115th Street apartment of 1945, hub of the early Beat circle

stops.name: New York, the forged prescription
stops.date_confidence: 1946 attested for the arrest for forging a narcotics prescription and the return to St. Louis under parental supervision (Wikipedia, 'William S. Burroughs'). Month and day default to 01; the pin is the Morningside Heights neighbourhood in which he was then living, not a courthouse.
stops.campa: He is arrested for writing a narcotics prescription in a doctor's name, and released into his parents' custody to dry out in St. Louis under supervision. Until now the machinery of the state has been something he read about. The sequence that starts here runs for the next fifteen years and does not vary much: an arrest, a family intervention, a change of address, then a change of country. Nothing about it stops him using. When the supervision ends he goes to Texas.
suggested_refs: The 1914 Harrison Narcotics Tax Act, the statute under which the prescription offence was charged

stops.name: Pharr, the Rio Grande Valley: the farm and the accumulator
stops.date_confidence: the part-ownership of Valley land with Kells Elvins is attested for 1946-1949 (Beatdom, 'Billy Burroughs: Gentleman Farmer'), and the birth of William S. Burroughs Jr. to Joan Vollmer at Conroe, Texas, is attested to 1947, month and day not given in the pool. The month here is an ordering device. Burroughs's use and construction of orgone accumulators from about 1949 is independently attested in his letters and the Reich literature but is not stated in reich.journey.json; the link is carried as reconstruction.
stops.campa: With Kells Elvins he part-owns citrus and cotton land in the Rio Grande Valley, and in a shed on the property he builds an orgone accumulator to Wilhelm Reich's published specification, a box of alternating organic and metallic layers meant to concentrate a life energy the Food and Drug Administration will shortly rule does not exist. He sits in it. He goes on believing in it for fifty years, through the injunction, the book burning, and Reich's death in a federal prison. That summer his son is born to Joan Vollmer at Conroe.
suggested_refs: Wilhelm Reich, The Cancer Biopathy (1948), the accumulator specification Burroughs built from
The 1954 FDA injunction against the orgone accumulator
sources: reich.journey.json, Forest Hills and Lewisburg stops

stops.name: 509 Wagner Street, Algiers: the house and the arrest
stops.date_confidence: the April 5, 1949 stop near Lee Circle, with unregistered handgun, marijuana, heroin and a Ginsberg letter about a marijuana sale, is attested (64 Parishes; New Orleans Historical). The pool's geography lens gave a coordinate about 1.2 km west of the house; the OpenStreetMap geocode for 509 Wagner Street is used. The pool's chronology lens dated the flight to Mexico to 1950; the arrest was 1949 and he crossed that autumn.
stops.campa: He buys a house across the river from the French Quarter and settles into morphine and paregoric, driving into the city to score. On the fifth of April 1949 New Orleans police stop his car near Lee Circle and find an unregistered handgun, marijuana, heroin, and a letter from Ginsberg about a marijuana sale. He is bailed. Louisiana is on the point of making possession a felony with a mandatory sentence, and his lawyer explains the arithmetic. That autumn he crosses into Mexico and does not come back for twenty-five years.
suggested_refs: 509 Wagner Street, Algiers, New Orleans
New Orleans Historical, on the Lee Circle stop of April 1949

stops.name: Cerrada de Medellin 37, Colonia Roma: the first address
stops.date_confidence: residence 1949-1950 attested by the pool's geography lens; the month is an ordering device for the autumn crossing. The street is today Calle Jose Alvarado 37, Roma Norte, and the OpenStreetMap geocode is used in place of the pool's coordinate, which sat about 700 metres northeast. The Kerouac and Cassady visit of 1950, in the same building, is attested.
stops.campa: The family takes rooms in a dead-end passage in Colonia Roma, behind the old Sears building. Mexico in 1949 is a country where a fugitive with dollars lives well and a permit costs a bribe; Burroughs says afterwards that anything he wanted was available there for money. Vollmer is on tequila and Benzedrine and her health is going. The children run in the street. In 1950 Kerouac and Neal Cassady turn up in the middle of a road trip and take rooms next door in the same building.
suggested_refs: Calle Jose Alvarado 37, Roma Norte, formerly Cerrada de Medellin 37
sources: Journey Mexico, 'Beatnik Fans Will Love Mexico City'

stops.name: Mexico City College, the codices and the calendar
stops.date_confidence: enrolment at Mexico City College under the G.I. Bill in 1950, to study Spanish and Mesoamerican manuscripts, is attested (Wikipedia, 'William S. Burroughs'). Month and day default to 01. The pin is the canonical atlas Mexico City coordinate shared with frida_kahlo.journey.json and diego_rivera.journey.json, used here because the stop is the study rather than a surviving campus address.
stops.campa: He enrols under the G.I. Bill to study Spanish, Mexican archaeology, and the Mayan codices, and he means it. The tuition is paid by the government of the country he is a fugitive from. The Dresden and Madrid manuscripts show him a priesthood running an entire agricultural society through a calendar that nobody outside the priesthood can read. That is the idea he uses for the rest of his working life: a control system is a book of dates, held by people who can read it, addressed to people who cannot.
suggested_refs: The Dresden and Madrid Maya codices, Burroughs's study material at Mexico City College

stops.name: Monterrey 122, the William Tell
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. The party was in John Healy's third-floor apartment above the Bounty Bar at Monterrey 122, Colonia Roma. The pool's own geography lens carried three errors corrected here: the coordinate was about 350 metres east of the street, Vollmer did not die at the scene but at the nearby Red Cross post, and Burroughs was thirty-seven, not twenty-eight. The thirteen days in custody and the later conviction in absentia for homicidio culposo, with a two-year suspended sentence, are attested (RealityStudio, Documents on the Death of Joan Vollmer Burroughs).
stops.campa: In John Healy's third-floor apartment above the Bounty Bar, on an afternoon of gin, Burroughs takes out a .380 Star automatic and tells his wife to put a glass on her head. He is thirty-seven. She is twenty-eight, and she puts the glass on her head. He fires from about two metres and hits her in the forehead. She is carried out and dies at the Red Cross post a few streets away while he waits outside. He is held thirteen days, bailed through a bribed lawyer, and convicted later in absentia of culpable homicide.
suggested_refs: RealityStudio, 'Documents on the Death of Joan Vollmer Burroughs', the contemporary Mexican police and press record
Jorge Garcia-Robles, The Stray Bullet: William S. Burroughs in Mexico (2013)
sources: RealityStudio, 'Documents on the Death of Joan Vollmer Burroughs'

stops.name: Palm Beach, the bail jumped
stops.date_confidence: the flight from Mexico at the end of 1952 to his parents in Palm Beach, Florida, and the departure from there for Bogota in January 1953, are attested in the pool's verified corrections against the claim that he returned to St. Louis. The month is an ordering device; the exact date of the crossing is not in the record consulted.
stops.campa: The case drags on. His own lawyer flees the country after shooting a teenager, and the two-year suspended sentence is eventually handed down to an empty chair. Before that Burroughs jumps bail and goes to his parents in Florida, who are running a gift shop and raising his son, because he is not raising him. He has just written Queer in Mexico City, a short book about wanting somebody who does not want you back, and he will not be able to publish it for thirty-three years. In January he leaves for Panama.
suggested_refs: Queer (written 1952, published 1985)
sources: RealityStudio, 'Documents on the Death of Joan Vollmer Burroughs'

stops.name: Panama City, the staging point
stops.date_confidence: January 1953 attested for the start of the South American leg (Literary Traveler, 'The Most Complete Derangement'; The Yage Letters, 1963). Day defaults to 01.
stops.campa: He goes south after yage, the Amazonian vine that the botanist Richard Evans Schultes has been collecting and that the newspapers say the Russians are testing for thought control. Burroughs wants it for the same reason the rumour says they do. A drug that opens one mind to another is not an experience, it is a communications technology, and he intends to test the claim on his own body. Panama is where he waits for papers, in a canal town of bars and cheap hotels, writing to Ginsberg that the whole thing may turn out to be a hoax.
suggested_refs: The Yage Letters (San Francisco: City Lights, 1963), the Panama and Colombia correspondence

stops.name: Bogota, the letters to Ginsberg
stops.date_confidence: 1953 attested; the month is an ordering device within the expedition. The letters themselves are the primary record and were published as The Yage Letters in 1963.
stops.campa: From Bogota he attaches himself to a plant-collecting expedition, to get upriver on somebody else's budget. Through every failure he goes on insisting that the drug is not a feeling but a channel, something to transmit and receive on, and that if it works at all the consequences are not private ones. The letters he sends from here become The Yage Letters a decade later, half field report and half performance: the botany, the officials, the boys, the dysentery, the sessions that produce nothing.
suggested_refs: The Yage Letters (1963), the Bogota datelines
sources: Reason.com, 'A Beatnik Tourist in Ayahuasca Country'

stops.name: Puerto Asis, the vine on the Putumayo
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to the exact site. The Putumayo basin is attested and the letters are datelined from the western Putumayo, reached by way of Cali, Popayan and Pasto; the pool's geography lens carried a coordinate some 120 km east, toward Puerto Leguizamo, which he did not use as a base. Puerto Asis is used as the nearest attested base. Month and day are an ordering device.
stops.campa: By way of Cali, Popayan and Pasto he reaches the western Putumayo, and on the river a curandero prepares the vine for him. He vomits, sees blue substance, and passes through what he writes down as the composite city where all human potentials are spread out in a vast silent market. The passage goes almost intact into Naked Lunch six years later. He does not get the cure he came for and does not claim to have got it. Which village it happened in he never names in the letters.
suggested_refs: The Yage Letters (1963), the Putumayo sessions
The 'composite city' passage as it appears in Naked Lunch (1959)

stops.name: New York, Junkie under the name William Lee
stops.date_confidence: 1953 attested for publication by Ace Books under the pseudonym William Lee (Wikipedia, 'William S. Burroughs'). The month is an ordering device and the pin is the publisher's midtown Manhattan address rather than a place Burroughs stood in.
stops.campa: Ace Books issues his first novel as a thirty-five-cent paperback bound back to back with a narcotics agent's memoir, under the name William Lee, with a publisher's preface warning the reader that the opinions in it are not the publisher's own. Junkie: Confessions of an Unredeemed Drug Addict sells a hundred thousand copies and earns its author almost nothing. His own name is nowhere on it. The allowance from St. Louis is still arriving every month, and he is thirty-nine years old.
suggested_refs: Junkie: Confessions of an Unredeemed Drug Addict (New York: Ace Books, 1953), the Ace Double edition

stops.name: Tangier, arrival in the International Zone
stops.date_confidence: January 1954, by way of Rome and Alan Ansen, after leaving New York in late 1953. The pool's chronology lens gave November 1954, which is not supported by Miles or by the letters chronology and is not followed. Day defaults to 01. The pin is the canonical atlas Tangier coordinate, shared with isabelle_eberhardt.journey.json.
stops.campa: He arrives in the International Zone in January, by way of Rome, into a city administered by nine powers at once and therefore by none of them: no exchange control, no drug law worth enforcing, banks and smugglers and refugees and a boy economy conducted in the open. Nine administrations mean no single voice giving orders, which is the condition he has been looking for since Harvard. He calls the place Interzone within months, and he stays four years.
suggested_refs: Interzone (1989), the assembled Tangier material
sources: Yabiladi, 'When American intellectuals chose Tangier as an exile'

stops.name: Villa Muniria, room 9
stops.date_confidence: residence 1954-1958 attested, with the room 9 attribution supported by the hotel's own record and by Beyond the Lamp Post, 'Hotel El-Muniria'. The pool's geography lens gave a coordinate about 850 metres south-southwest; the OpenStreetMap geocode for the hotel is used. Month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: In a cheap pension above the harbour he takes room 9 and works on majoun and the German opioid Eukodol, injecting up to fifteen times a day and letting the finished pages fall on the floor where he drops them. He writes routines rather than chapters: self-contained obscene sketches with no order and no narrator apologising for them. He weighs under fifty kilos and does not change his clothes. He says afterwards that he has almost no memory of composing the book, only of the floor filling up.
suggested_refs: Hotel El Muniria, 1 Rue Magellan, Tangier, room 9

stops.name: 99 Cromwell Road, London: the apomorphine cure
stops.date_confidence: spring 1956, and he travelled from Tangier at his father's urging (Filter, 'Why the Curious Story of William S. Burroughs' Heroin Cure Still Matters'). The pool's chronology lens dated the cure to 1960 and had him arriving from Paris; both are wrong and the geography lens, which has 1956, is followed. Dent ran the programme from two rented floors of a nursing home at 99 Cromwell Road, SW7; the pool's coordinate was about 3.4 km away in Mayfair.
stops.campa: At his father's urging he leaves Tangier for London and puts himself in the hands of Dr John Yerbury Dent, who treats addiction with apomorphine, a morphine derivative that produces no euphoria and, on Dent's account, regulates the vomiting centre back toward normal metabolism. Dent runs the programme out of two rented floors of a Kensington nursing home. The cure holds. Burroughs will campaign for apomorphine for the next forty years, in prefaces, letters and interviews, against a medical profession that shows no interest in it whatever.
suggested_refs: John Yerbury Dent, Anxiety and Its Treatment (1941)
Burroughs's 'Letter from a Master Addict to Dangerous Drugs', British Journal of Addiction (1957)
sources: Filter, 'Why the Curious Story of William S. Burroughs' Heroin Cure Still Matters'

stops.name: Tangier, the manuscript typed on the floor
stops.date_confidence: 1957 attested for the Ginsberg and Kerouac visit and the typing and sequencing of the Naked Lunch manuscript in Tangier (Wikipedia, 'William S. Burroughs'). Month is an ordering device. The final assembly was completed in Paris in 1959 by Ginsberg, Alan Ansen, Gysin and Sinclair Beiles.
stops.campa: Ginsberg, Peter Orlovsky and Kerouac come to Tangier and set to work on the floor of room 9. Kerouac types the pages, has nightmares from what he is typing, and supplies the title out of a misheard phrase: the frozen moment when everyone sees what is on the end of every fork. Alan Ansen arrives to help. Nobody in the room can say what order the routines belong in. Burroughs's position, then and for the rest of his life, is that the order does not matter, and he has as yet no method for saying why.
suggested_refs: The Naked Lunch typescripts, Berg Collection, New York Public Library

segments.name: The Beat Hotel and the Cut-Up

stops.name: 9 rue Git-le-Coeur, room 15
stops.date_confidence: January 1958, when Ginsberg found him the room (Barry Miles, The Beat Hotel: Ginsberg, Burroughs and Corso in Paris, 1957-1963). The pool's chronology lens gave 1959, a year late, and the geography lens inverted the room numbers: 15 was Burroughs's own room, and Gysin worked in 25. Day defaults to 01.
stops.campa: Ginsberg finds him a room in a no-star hotel on a short street off the Seine: forty-two rooms, a squat toilet on each landing, hot water on Thursdays, and a landlady who tolerates everything short of arson. Burroughs takes room 15 and stays five years. Along the corridor is the painter and writer Brion Gysin, whom he had met in Tangier in 1954 and disliked on sight. In this building they begin working together, and they go on doing it for the next thirty years.
suggested_refs: Barry Miles, The Beat Hotel: Ginsberg, Burroughs and Corso in Paris, 1957-1963 (2000)
sources: Culturedarm.com, 'William Burroughs, Brion Gysin, and the Beat Hotel'

stops.name: Chicago, the Chicago Review excerpt
stops.date_confidence: 1958 attested for the Chicago Review excerpt, the resulting controversy, and the departure of the editor Irving Rosenthal (Wikipedia, 'William S. Burroughs'). Month is an ordering device; the pin is the University of Chicago, the magazine's home.
stops.campa: The Chicago Review, a student quarterly at the University of Chicago, prints ten pages of the Tangier routines. A columnist in the Chicago Daily News calls the issue filthy, the university leans on the editors, and the winter number is stopped before it can be printed. The editor Irving Rosenthal resigns with most of his staff and takes the material to a new magazine, Big Table, whose first issue the Post Office impounds. The book itself still has no publisher anywhere.
suggested_refs: Chicago Review, Autumn 1958
Big Table 1 (1959) and the Post Office seizure

stops.name: Paris, Olympia Press prints Naked Lunch
stops.date_confidence: July 1959 publication attested (Columbia University Libraries, 'Naked Lunch: the First Fifty Years'). Day defaults to 01. The pin is the canonical atlas Paris coordinate, shared with diego_rivera.journey.json; Olympia's office at 7 rue Saint-Severin geocodes to 48.8526, 2.3443, and the pool's own coordinate for it was about 500 metres off and matched no known Olympia address.
stops.campa: Maurice Girodias, who publishes Lolita and Beckett and a large catalogue of frank pornography out of an office off the rue Saint-Severin, reads the manuscript, decides he wants it in a fortnight, and gets it. Naked Lunch appears in Paris in July 1959 in the green wrappers of the Traveller's Companion series, sold to tourists, three years before any American house will touch it. Part of the final sequence of the routines is settled by the order in which the pages come back from the printer.
stops.quote: Junk is the ideal product . . . the ultimate merchandise. No sales talk necessary. The client will crawl through a sewer and beg to buy.
stops.quote_source: William S. Burroughs, 'Deposition: Testimony Concerning a Sickness' (1960), appended to later editions of Naked Lunch
suggested_refs: Naked Lunch (Paris: Olympia Press, Traveller's Companion Series, 1959)
Columbia University Libraries, 'Naked Lunch: the First Fifty Years'
sources: Columbia University Libraries, 'Naked Lunch: the First Fifty Years'

stops.name: Beat Hotel, the razor through the newspapers
stops.date_confidence: autumn 1959 attested for the discovery and for Burroughs's adoption of the method. Gysin made the cut alone in his own room and brought the result to Burroughs, who had just returned from London that September; the pool's geography lens has Burroughs watching it happen, which no source supports. Day defaults to 01.
stops.campa: Trimming a mounted drawing with a blade in his own room, Gysin cuts through the stack of newspapers under it and finds the sliced columns reading across into sentences nobody wrote. He carries them down the corridor. Burroughs does not treat it as a parlour game. If a sentence can be cut and the halves recombined into sense, then sense was never the property of the writer, and the sentences already running inside a human head can be cut the same way. He begins cutting everything: his own pages, the newspapers, Rimbaud, Shakespeare, Kafka.
stops.quote: The simplest cut/up cuts a page down the middle and across the middle into four sections. Section 1 is then placed with section 4 and section 3 with section 2 in a new sequence.
stops.quote_source: William S. Burroughs, The Electronic Revolution (1970), describing the method
suggested_refs: Brion Gysin and William S. Burroughs, Minutes to Go (Paris: Two Cities Editions, 1960)
'The Cut-Up Method of Brion Gysin' (1961)
sources: Culturedarm.com, 'William Burroughs, Brion Gysin, and the Beat Hotel'
The Job: interviews with Daniel Odier (1969)

stops.name: Paris, The Soft Machine
stops.date_confidence: 1961 publication by Olympia Press attested. Month and day default to 01; the pin is the canonical atlas Paris coordinate. The quotation is widely misattributed to Nova Express; a full text of Nova Express was checked and does not contain the sequence, which closes 'The Mayan Caper' in The Soft Machine.
stops.campa: Olympia prints the first volume of what becomes the Nova trilogy, built almost entirely out of cut-up and fold-in worked on his own accumulated pages. The soft machine is the human body, and the argument buried in the wreckage of the syntax is that the body has been colonised by parasites who operate through word and image. In the section called The Mayan Caper an agent travels back in time and burns the priests' control calendar. It is the Mexico City College reading list, turned into a raid.
stops.quote: Cut word lines—Cut music lines—Smash the control images—Smash the control machine—Burn the books—Kill the priests—Kill! Kill! Kill!
stops.quote_source: William S. Burroughs, The Soft Machine (Paris: Olympia Press, 1961), closing lines of 'The Mayan Caper'
suggested_refs: The Soft Machine (Paris: Olympia Press, 1961), 'The Mayan Caper'
sources: Wikiquote and LibQuotes book-specific entries for The Soft Machine

stops.name: Paris, The Ticket That Exploded
stops.date_confidence: 1962 publication by Olympia Press attested; month and day default to 01, and the pin is the canonical atlas Paris coordinate. The closing sentences of the campa reach past Burroughs's death in 1997 to prompt injection in multi-agent language-model systems. That forward reach is not a lifetime event and is not something Burroughs is on record about in any form; it is carried under the forward grant recorded for him in EXCEPTIONS.md, ruled by the author on 2026-08-17 and limited there to one or two sentences closing a stop that is otherwise entirely his own. Primary sources for the machine material: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications, prompt injection entry; arXiv 2410.07283, 'Prompt Infection: LLM-to-LLM Prompt Injection within Multi-Agent Systems' (2024); Simon Willison on prompt injection (2023-2024).
stops.campa: The second Nova volume states the thesis without metaphor. The word is a virus: an organism that entered the human nervous system, established itself so completely that it is now mistaken for the host, and reproduces by making its carriers speak. Try to stop the inner voice for ten seconds and something in you resists. Six decades later, engineers hardening assemblies of language models find that text handed from one agent to another can carry instructions that capture the second agent and travel on through the third. Burroughs is not on record about machines.
stops.quote: The word is now a virus. The flu virus may once have been a healthy lung cell. It is now a parasitic organism that invades and damages the lungs. The word may once have been a healthy neural cell. It is now a parasitic organism that invades and damages the central nervous system. Modern man has lost the option of silence. Try halting sub-vocal speech. Try to achieve even ten seconds of inner silence. You will encounter a resisting organism that forces you to talk. That organism is the word.
stops.quote_source: William S. Burroughs, The Ticket That Exploded (New York: Grove Press, 1962), pp. 49-50, the 'operation rewrite' section

stops.name: Grove Press, New York: the American edition and the prosecutions
stops.date_confidence: 1962 attested for the Grove Press edition and the obscenity prosecutions it triggered. Month is an ordering device; the pin is Grove's office at 64 University Place.
stops.campa: Barney Rosset issues Naked Lunch in the United States and the prosecutions start at once: Boston, Los Angeles, booksellers arrested, stock seized. Grove has already carried Lady Chatterley's Lover and Tropic of Cancer through the federal courts and treats the litigation as a line in the publishing budget. The Massachusetts case will run all the way to the state's highest court. Burroughs is in Europe for most of it, and contributes to his own defence an essay about addiction rather than about obscenity.
stops.quote: You see control can never be a means to any practical end. . . . Control can never be a means to anything but more control . . . like Junk.
suggested_refs: Naked Lunch (New York: Grove Press, 1962)
Attorney General v. A Book Named 'Naked Lunch'

stops.name: New York, Nova Express
stops.date_confidence: 1964 publication by Grove Press attested; month and day default to 01. The pin is the publisher's office. The pool's afterlife lens listed the trilogy in the wrong order and gave the title as 'The Nova Express'; the sequence is The Soft Machine (1961), The Ticket That Exploded (1962), Nova Express (1964), and the third takes no definite article.
stops.campa: Grove prints the third Nova volume, which arranges the cosmology as a police procedural. The Nova Mob are parasites who arrived from outer space and hold the planet by controlling its word and image lines; the Nova Police move against them by cutting those lines. It reads as science fiction. In the interviews of these years Burroughs says repeatedly that it is not written as science fiction: he takes himself to be describing how control on this planet actually works, in the only vocabulary that has words for it.
suggested_refs: Nova Express (New York: Grove Press, 1964)

stops.name: Boston, the Supreme Judicial Court
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. The Commonwealth proceeded against the book itself; four of the seven justices found it grossly offensive and the court nonetheless held it not legally obscene (Harvard Crimson, 'Naked Lunch Judged Not Legally Obscene'; Attorney General v. A Book Named 'Naked Lunch').
stops.campa: The Commonwealth of Massachusetts sues the book itself, a proceeding in rem against an object with no rights to assert, and Norman Mailer, Allen Ginsberg and John Ciardi testify for the defence of it. On the seventh of July the Supreme Judicial Court rules that Naked Lunch, which four of the seven justices call grossly offensive, is not obscene within the constitutional test. It is the last major obscenity trial in the United States over a work made of words alone. Burroughs is in London and does not attend.
suggested_refs: Attorney General v. A Book Named 'Naked Lunch', 351 Mass. 298 (1966)
sources: Harvard Crimson, 'Naked Lunch Judged Not Legally Obscene'
casemine.com, Attorney General v. Naked Lunch

stops.name: Dalmeny Court, Duke Street: The Invisible Generation
stops.date_confidence: the essay appeared in 1966 in IT and the Los Angeles Free Press; no month is given in the pool and the month here is an ordering device only. The Duke Street flat, in Dalmeny Court, dates from 1966/67 to 1973/74; the pool's geography lens dated it 1956-1960, a decade early, and separately anchored the essay to Portobello Road some five kilometres away.
stops.campa: He takes a flat in Dalmeny Court, on Duke Street in St James's, around the corner from Fortnum and Mason, and works there through most of the next eight years. From it he publishes The Invisible Generation in the underground paper IT and the Los Angeles Free Press: not an essay but a set of instructions, for putting cheap tape recorders into enough hands to cut a president's speech with coughs and snarls and animal noise and play the result back in the street, the subway, the station, the rally. He calls the effect waking suggestion, and insists it is not subliminal.
suggested_refs: 'The Invisible Generation', International Times and Los Angeles Free Press (1966), reprinted in The Job

stops.name: Saint Hill Manor, East Grinstead: the model control system
stops.date_confidence: an intensive course of roughly two months in the first half of 1968, reaching the state the organisation calls Clear (Tony Ortega, 'William Burroughs at Scientology's Saint Hill Manor in 1968'). The month is an ordering device. The pool's geography lens carried a longitude of the wrong sign, landing about 2.5 km east of the estate; the OpenStreetMap geocode is used.
stops.campa: He enrols at L. Ron Hubbard's world headquarters in Sussex, takes an intensive two-month course, and reaches the rank the organisation calls Clear. The interest is genuine. The E-meter, and the auditing of a recorded trauma until it loses its charge, sit close enough to his own practice that he wants to see the machinery from inside. Then he publishes against it, and calls Scientology a model control system, a state in fact with its own courts, police, rewards and penalties.
suggested_refs: Burroughs's Scientology articles collected in Ali's Smile / Naked Scientology (1978)
Douglas Kahn, 'Cellular Phones: Corporeal Communications Technologies in William S. Burroughs and L. Ron Hubbard'

stops.name: London, The Electronic Revolution goes to press
stops.date_confidence: first published 1970 by Expanded Media Editions in West Germany, bilingual English and German; the Cambridge printing on Ian Ormiston's Blackmoor Head Press, fifty signed copies with Gysin silkscreens for Henri Chopin's Collection OU, is the 1971 second edition and the pool's chronology lens conflated the two. The pin is Burroughs's own London flat, where the material was written, not the publisher's city. Month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: Expanded Media Editions brings out The Electronic Revolution in West Germany, in English and German, a short book that takes the tape method out of the poetry magazines and points it at institutions. Word and image are viruses, he writes, and this is not a comparison offered for effect. Cut the associational lines the mass media lay down and the associations break. The following year a Cambridge hand press runs off fifty signed copies with silkscreens by Gysin.
stops.quote: I have frequently spoken of word and image as viruses or as acting as viruses, and this is not an allegorical comparison.
stops.quote_source: William S. Burroughs, The Electronic Revolution (Expanded Media Editions, 1970)
suggested_refs: The Electronic Revolution (Expanded Media Editions, 1970; Blackmoor Head Press, Cambridge, 1971)
The Job: interviews with Daniel Odier (1969)
sources: UbuWeb ubuclassics edition of The Electronic Revolution (2005), p. 14

stops.name: Moka Bar, Frith Street: the playback operation
stops.date_confidence: 1972 attested for the operation and the closure some months later (Wikipedia, 'William S. Burroughs'; Museum of American Poetics). Only the year is given in the pool, so month and day default to 01, though Burroughs's own published account gives specific dates in the summer of that year. The pin is the bar's Soho address.
stops.campa: After what he describes as outrageous and unprovoked discourtesy from the staff of an espresso bar on Frith Street in Soho, Burroughs stands on the pavement outside it with a camera and a tape recorder, photographing the front and recording the street, and comes back on later days to play the recordings back at the door. The bar closes that autumn. He publishes the operation afterwards as a case study, with dates and times, in the flat register of a field report.
stops.quote: You can cut the mutter line of the mass media and put the altered mutter line out in the streets with a tape recorder.
stops.quote_source: William S. Burroughs, The Electronic Revolution (1970), p. 14
suggested_refs: Burroughs's own account of the Moka Bar operation, reprinted in The Adding Machine (1985)
sources: UbuWeb ubuclassics edition of The Electronic Revolution (2005), p. 14

stops.name: City College, New York: the return and the withdrawal
stops.date_confidence: 1974 attested for the return to the United States, the teaching post Ginsberg arranged at City College of New York, and a medically supervised withdrawal from heroin (Wikipedia, 'William S. Burroughs'). The month is an ordering device for the spring semester.
stops.campa: Broke and out of print in his own country, he comes back to New York, where Ginsberg has arranged a teaching post at City College: one semester of talking to students about writing, for a fee, which he loathes doing and does. He withdraws from heroin again under medical supervision. He is sixty years old. James Grauerholz arrives from Kansas at twenty-three, makes himself his manager, and begins booking the reading tours that will support him for the next twenty-three years.
suggested_refs: The Job and the reading-tour circuit organised by James Grauerholz from 1974

stops.name: 222 Bowery, the Bunker
stops.date_confidence: residence from 1974 attested; John Giorno found him the room in a former YMCA, windowless and steel-doored (Gothamist; Ephemeral New York). Month is an ordering device. The pool's geography lens claimed the whole late trilogy was written here; only Cities of the Red Night (1981) was largely written at the Bunker, the two later volumes in Lawrence.
stops.campa: John Giorno tells him about an empty room in a former YMCA on the Bowery: windowless, painted white, a steel door, a locker room with a row of urinals still standing in it. Burroughs takes it and calls it the Bunker. He keeps a machete by the bed and an orgone accumulator in the corner, and writes most of Cities of the Red Night in the white room, still cutting and splicing fifteen years after the Beat Hotel. Patti Smith, Debbie Harry, Lou Reed and later Basquiat come through it.
suggested_refs: Cities of the Red Night (New York: Holt, Rinehart and Winston, 1981)
222 Bowery, preserved after 1997 by John Giorno
sources: Clio, Former Residence of William S. Burroughs

stops.name: DeLand, Florida: the death of the son
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day and the hour. He was found on 2 March in a ditch beside a DeLand highway and died at 6:35 the next morning of acute gastrointestinal haemorrhage with micronodular cirrhosis, following his 1976 liver transplant. The pool's chronology lens gave the place as 'Deer Lodge, Florida', which does not exist.
stops.campa: William S. Burroughs Jr., who published two novels of his own, received a liver transplant at twenty-nine and never stopped drinking, is found on the second of March in a ditch beside a DeLand highway and dies the next morning at twenty-five past six of gastrointestinal haemorrhage with cirrhosis. He is thirty-three years old. His father was not raising him when Joan Vollmer died, and did not raise him afterwards. Burroughs outlives him by sixteen years.
suggested_refs: William S. Burroughs Jr., Speed (1970) and Kentucky Ham (1973)

stops.name: 1927 Learnard Avenue, Lawrence: the last address
stops.date_confidence: residence in Lawrence from 1981 to 1997 attested, with James Grauerholz as manager and companion. The month is an ordering device. The pool's geography lens gave a coordinate about 850 metres north of the house; the OpenStreetMap geocode for 1927 Learnard Avenue is used.
stops.campa: Grauerholz moves him out of New York to a small white bungalow in Kansas, two blocks from the river, with a garden, a fishpond, and in time six cats. He keeps a methadone prescription, a shotgun, and a daily journal. He had been in New York seven years and does not go back to live there. In Lawrence he writes The Place of Dead Roads and The Western Lands, sees almost nobody he has not chosen to see, and becomes a local fixture whom students point out to each other in the liquor store.
suggested_refs: The Place of Dead Roads (1983) and The Western Lands (1987), both written in Lawrence
Last Words: The Final Journals of William S. Burroughs (2000)
sources: KCUR, 'William S. Burroughs And Lawrence, Kansas'

stops.name: Lawrence, the shotgun paintings and the bypass
stops.date_confidence: the triple coronary bypass is attested to June 1991 and David Cronenberg's Naked Lunch to a December 1991 release. The shotgun paintings date from the late 1980s onward and are grouped here rather than dated precisely; the day defaults to 01.
stops.campa: He begins firing shotguns at plywood panels backed with cans of spray paint, and the punctured, splattered boards sell in galleries in New York and Europe, which he finds neither surprising nor absurd. The blast makes a mark he did not compose. It is the same argument as the razor through the newspapers, made with a heavier tool. In June he undergoes a triple coronary bypass at seventy-seven. In December, David Cronenberg's film of Naked Lunch opens, with the killing of Joan Vollmer written into it as the engine of the whole book.
suggested_refs: Naked Lunch, dir. David Cronenberg (1991)
The shotgun paintings, exhibited from 1987 onward

stops.name: Lawrence, the record made with Kurt Cobain
stops.date_confidence: 1993 attested for 'The Priest' They Called Him, recorded in two places and assembled; the collaborations with Ministry, Laurie Anderson and R.E.M. and the 1994 Nike commercial belong to the same years. Month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: Kurt Cobain records a guitar part in Seattle over a reading Burroughs has taped in Kansas, and the two halves are pressed together on a ten-inch record without the two men ever having been in the same room for it. They meet once, later, in Lawrence. Ministry, Laurie Anderson and R.E.M. work with him in the same stretch of years, and in 1994 a Nike commercial puts his face on American television. He is seventy-nine, and has become a voice to a generation that has not read a page of him.
suggested_refs: 'The Priest' They Called Him, William S. Burroughs and Kurt Cobain (Tim/Kerr Records, 1993)
sources: Wikipedia, 'William S. Burroughs', discography and collaborations

stops.name: Lawrence Memorial Hospital, the last day
stops.date_confidence: attested. He suffered a heart attack on 1 August 1997 and died on 2 August in the hospital's intensive care unit, aged eighty-three (Washington Post obituary, 4 August 1997). The pool's chronology and geography lenses both had him dying at the house on Learnard Avenue, which the obituary record contradicts.
stops.campa: He has a heart attack on the first of August and dies the following day in the intensive care unit, aged eighty-three. He has lived in Kansas sixteen years, longer than he lived anywhere after childhood. The death certificate gives complications of a heart attack suffered the previous day. Grauerholz is with him. The cats are at the house on Learnard Avenue, two miles away, where he had been working that week on the journals that are published three years later.
suggested_refs: Washington Post obituary, 4 August 1997
Last Words: The Final Journals of William S. Burroughs (2000)
sources: Harvard Crimson, 'Writer, Beat Icon Burroughs Dead at 83'

stops.name: Bellefontaine Cemetery, the family plot
stops.date_confidence: burial at Bellefontaine Cemetery, St. Louis, in the Burroughs family lot is attested (Find a Grave); the exact day of interment is not given in the sources consulted and is an ordering device. Both the geography and afterlife lenses in the pool carried a coordinate about 2.2 km southeast of the cemetery grounds; the OpenStreetMap geocode for 4947 West Florissant Avenue is used.
stops.campa: He is buried in the family lot in St. Louis, a few miles from the house he was born in. The tall obelisk in the plot reads WILLIAM S. BURROUGHS and belongs to his grandfather, the one who built the adding machine; visitors mistake it for the writer's grave every year. His own marker lies flat nearby and gives his dates and two words: American Writer. It does not say how he came to be one. He had answered that himself twelve years earlier, in print, in the introduction to a book he wrote in Mexico City in 1952.
stops.quote: I am forced to the appalling conclusion that I would never have become a writer but for Joan's death, and to a realization of the extent to which this event has motivated and formulated my writing. I live with the constant threat of possession, and a constant need to escape from possession, from Control. So the death of Joan brought me in contact with the invader, the Ugly Spirit, and maneuvered me into a lifelong struggle, in which I have had no choice except to write my way out.
stops.quote_source: William S. Burroughs, introduction to Queer, February 1985
suggested_refs: Bellefontaine Cemetery, 4947 West Florissant Avenue, St. Louis, the Burroughs family lot
Introduction to Queer (1985)
